subject: 1AD5A5F58C9D4D80A982ED7AA5435D7E
introduction: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quoted the sentence in letter after letter to early Western believers, and these readings gather his uses of it with related passages from Bahá’u’lláh. He reads it this way: the call is God’s justice, and goes to all; being chosen is His favour, and cannot be earned. Faith “is a token of grace.” Yet the chosen are also described as those who had capacity, who heard and responded, who stretched out a hand for the cup; and nearly every letter turns from the statement to its use: give thanks, and arise to serve. Election is one of the most disputed ideas in religion, and the outside quotations show why. Paul and the Qur’án state God’s freedom as strongly as the readings do. Moses tells Israel it was not chosen for its merit, Amos that being chosen means being held to account, and Jesus that much is required where much is given. Peter learns that “God is no respecter of persons.” And Burns’s Holy Willie and the Pharisee in the Temple show what the doctrine becomes when the gratitude is taken out of it.
questions: “By justice all are called, but by Mercy a few are especially chosen.” Put the distinction in your own words. Does it answer the charge that election is unfair?
The readings say faith is a gift, and also that the chosen had “ability and capacity.” Where have you seen grace and effort meet?
Almost every letter ends in “thank God.” Why is gratitude the response asked for, and how is it different from the Pharisee’s “I thank thee, that I am not as other men”?
Amos: “You only have I known … therefore I will punish you.” What responsibilities come with believing oneself chosen?
Peter concluded that “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted.” How should the chosen regard those who have not responded?
A lost speck of jewel “would assuredly” be found. What does this last reading add to a guide that has spoken so much of the few?

outside.why: “Faith, which is life eternal, is a token of grace and not the result of justice.” Paul: by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.
Love burns “by the power of attraction and not through human effort and striving.” Paul: it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.

Effort does acquire “knowledge, learning and other perfections.” Paul holds both in one sentence: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you. How do you divide the work in your own experience?
“The elect of humanity are those who live together in love and unity.” John gives the same test: he that loveth his brother abideth in the light.
The saying on which the guide turns. Jesus, at the end of a parable about a feast: for many are called, but few are chosen.
The parable it concludes: a king sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come; they made light of it.
“The gift of faith is a bestowal emanating from absolute mercy.” Jesus: no man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.
The called show justice, the chosen favour; “He does as He wills.” The word to Moses that Paul quotes: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.

Burns put the doctrine in the mouth of a hypocrite at his prayers: thou sends ane to Heaven and ten to Hell, a’ for thy glory, and no for onie guid or ill they’ve done afore thee. What keeps a belief in being chosen from becoming Holy Willie’s?

“By justice all are called, but by Mercy a few are especially chosen.” Peter, after a vision that overturned his idea of who was chosen: God is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. How do the two statements fit together?
“He appropriateth by His mercy those whom He liketh.” The Qur’án, to a Prophet who could not bring his own uncle to believe: thou guidest not whom thou lovest, but Allah guideth whom He will.

The friends “have been endowed with ability and capacity, on which account they became of the chosen.” The parable’s last scene, in which one who came is found unready: friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?
“The transformation depends upon divine bounty.” Isaiah: I am found of them that sought me not.

“Only a special number will have this attainment … It will always be so.” Paul speaks of what God wills: who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. Is the fewness of the chosen a fact about God’s will or about human response?

God “has always chosen certain souls.” Moses told Israel why it was not their merit: the Lord did not choose you because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest; but because the Lord loved you.
“This plenty is a special favor.” Paul’s question to anyone inclined to take credit: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?
The divine table is spread, yet “those who were invited did not respond.” Luke’s version of the feast: they all with one consent began to make excuse.
Jesus’s advice to hosts in the same chapter says who will come: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind.
“All but a few remain bereft of this celestial city.” Asked whether few are saved, Jesus turned the question into a command: strive to enter in at the strait gate.
The Youth holds out the Chalice, “wondering what eye will recognize His glory.” The letter to Laodicea: behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door.
Grace falls “even as the rains in spring,” but the withered are deprived. The parable of the sower: the seed is the same; the soils differ.
Some birds flew to the Kingdom; others “were afflicted with weariness and lassitude.” Jesus: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
“The Pen of the Most High is unceasingly calling; and yet, how few … have inclined their ear.” Proverbs: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets.
Few “can comprehend the stations of God’s favors.” Jesus to those who did: blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.
Outward faith is common; “cognizant faith” is rare. The Qur’án: say “We submit,” for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts.
True faith, where it exists, “cannot be destroyed.” Paul’s chain: whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
A saying that no true followers exist, or only a handful. Paul on Israel: there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then is it no more of works.
“All the people are sleep but you are awake.” Paul: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.

“We are the blessed ones who know.” The Pharisee in the Temple thought so too: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are. How do the readings’ repeated calls to thankfulness guard against his prayer?
“The chosen have heard and understood the call.” Jesus: my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
The whole world cries “O Thou the Desired One!”, and turns away when He appears. John: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
“How many an ignorant one hath attained, and how many a learned one hath been barred!” Jesus: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
“You were neither ministers nor monks and you have attained this grace.” Paul: not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
James: hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith?
“We shall make their highest ones their lowest ones.” Matthew gives both sayings together: the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
The parable that precedes it, where those hired last are paid the same: friend, I do thee no wrong. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own?
True liberty is “complete servitude unto God.” Sinai made election conditional on the same thing: if ye will obey my voice indeed, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me.
All are heedless “except for a very few.” Jesus spoke to that small number without reproach for its size: fear not, little flock; for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.

“He made you one of the chosen ones and created you for the promotion of heavenly teachings.” Jesus: ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit.
“O ye whom God hath chosen from among those who are called.” Peter: ye are a chosen generation, that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness.
Chosen, and enabled “to perform righteous deeds.” Peter: give diligence to make your calling and election sure.

“Thou wert among those who were called and thou didst become one of the chosen.” Paul on his own case: by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all.

“God selects a few souls and bestows upon them His Special Gifts.” Amos told the chosen people what the gift entails: you only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities. What does being chosen cost?
“Consider how dear you were to God.” Jesus: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
Chosen, guided, and given glad tidings. Paul: walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness.
“God hath singled thee out for guidance.” Isaiah names the place of choosing: I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.
“Praise the one true God Who hath opened such a door.” The Qur’án: such is the bounty of Allah, which He bestoweth upon whom He will.
“Thank God, for that He hath made thee of the Chosen Ones.” Jesus on how an invited guest should carry himself: when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room.
“This is a station which God giveth to whomsoever He pleaseth.” The Qur’án: yet ye will not, unless Allah willeth.

Paul’s hardest image: hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? The readings speak only of gratitude in the chosen, never of the others as made for dishonour. What difference does that make?
A speck of jewel lost beneath a mountain would be found “in this Day.” Jesus: what man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not go after that which is lost, until he find it?

peter-calling-and-election-sure.text: Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall

romans-whom-he-called-them-he-justified.text: Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified

romans-remnant-according-to-grace.text: Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace

isaiah-found-of-them-that-sought-me-not.text: I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not: I said, Behold me, behold me, unto a nation that was not called by my name

luke-are-there-few-that-be-saved.text: Then said one unto him, Lord, are there few that be saved? And he said unto them, Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able

matthew-wedding-garment.text: And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth
